props.title: Gone Baby Gone
props.initialSlug: Detective hunts missing girl in Boston's dark underbelly

sections.content: Ben Affleck's directorial debut Gone Baby Gone masterfully adapts Dennis Lehane's gritty Boston crime novel. Like fellow Lehane adaptation Mystic River (2003), it digs deep into working-class Boston neighborhoods where moral choices aren't black and white. Casey Affleck's Patrick Kenzie carries the film's crushing ethical weight - when a child disappears, his investigation forces impossible decisions about right, wrong, and who should raise a child. The film follows Chinatown (1974) and L.A. Confidential (1997) in the tradition of neo-noir detective stories where solving the crime leads to devastating moral quandaries.

sections.content: Gone Baby Gone's Boston setting continues a rich tradition of Massachusetts crime films that capture the region's specific character and class dynamics. The Friends of Eddie Coyle (1973) pioneered this territory with its stark portrayal of small-time criminals. The Departed (2006) and The Town (2010) further explored Boston's criminal underworld through the lens of loyalty and betrayal. These films share an authentic sense of place and complex moral universe where good and evil blur. SUBHEAD: The Ethics of Investigation

Like other great detective noir films, Gone Baby Gone uses its investigation to probe deeper philosophical questions. Se7en (1995) confronted its detectives with evil that challenged their worldview. Memories of Murder (2003) showed how an unsolved case can haunt investigators. Casey Affleck's Patrick Kenzie joins these ranks of detectives forced to question whether uncovering the truth always serves justice. The film's devastating finale echoes Chinatown's (1974) bitter lesson that sometimes there are no right answers.
